content: The maxilla, also known in plural as maxillae, is formed by the fusion of two bones along the palatal fissure, creating the upper jaw. This anatomical structure is comparable to the mandible, which is similarly formed by the fusion of two halves at the mental symphysis. The alveolar process of the maxilla houses the upper teeth and is referred to as the maxillary arch. The maxilla connects laterally to the zygomatic bones, commonly known as the cheekbones. Additionally, the maxilla contributes to the formation of the boundaries of three cavities: the roof of the mouth, the floor and lateral wall of the nasal antrum, and the floor of the orbit. Furthermore, the maxilla plays a role in forming two fossae—the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae—and two fissures, namely the inferior orbital fissure and the pterygomaxillary fissure. Each half of the fused maxilla consists of the body of the maxilla and four processes: the zygomatic process, the frontal process, the alveolar process, and the palatine process. Additionally, the infraorbital foramen is a notable feature of the maxilla. The maxilla articulates with nine bones. Two of these are cranial bones: the frontal bone and the ethmoid bone. The remaining seven are facial bones: the nasal bone, zygomatic bone, lacrimal bone, inferior nasal concha, palatine bone, vomer, and the adjacent fused maxillary bone. Occasionally, the maxilla also articulates with the orbital surface and, in some cases, with the lateral pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone. Additional images of the maxilla include depictions of the seven bones that articulate to form the orbit, the facial bones, the outer surface of the left maxilla, the nasal surface of the left maxilla, the left maxillary sinus opened from the exterior, the bony palate and alveolar arch, the sphenoid bone visible at the center-right, the articulation of the left palatine bone with the maxilla, and a side view of the teeth and jaws.
